news.title: Extra:  Ending the NIL “Wild West” | Craig Carton On The Need For College Sports Reform
news.text:
The Senate has passed the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act by a vote of 77 to 22 in a sweeping effort to rein in college sports and the Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) landscape. With college football programs managing multi-million-dollar payrolls, unchecked transfer portals, and unregulated booster funding, Congress is attempting to establish order and set clear parameters. 

Outkick host Craig Carton joined Dave Anthony on The FOX News Rundown this past week to discuss how NIL evolved from fair athlete compensation into what he calls “the wild, wild west.” Carton breaks down the proposed reforms, including restrictions on transfer rules, caps on agency commissions, conference realignments, and how these changes will impact student-athletes, coaches, and college athletic programs moving forward. 

Carton also discusses his new show on Outkick, which blends sports, politics, and culture.

news.title: The curious timing of Ted Cruz’s Protect College Sports Act
news.text:
The Protect College Sports Act, sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and passed by the Senate this week, is ostensibly an effort to bring common-sense reform to an NCAA that, in pursuit of the almighty dollar, has abandoned all pretense of developing college athletes academically and personally. It’s hard to pinpoint when the cries to fix college sports got so loud, but one especially hears it everywhere NCAA Division I football teams compete on Saturdays.

But no matter how it looks on its face, the bill is a deeply flawed attempt at reforming college sports “because its framework confers consequential legal and economic benefits on institutions that already exercise enormous power,” NAACP President Derrick Johnson wrote to Senate leaders in August. Johnson argued that the bill could be catastrophic for Black student-athletes, who make up the majority of FBS football and Division I men’s basketball rosters and have already suffered decades of economic harm under the NCAA’s former rules.

It’s hard to pinpoint when the cries to fix college sports got so loud, but one especially hears it everywhere NCAA Division I football teams compete on Saturdays.

Among other things, the Congressional Research Service’s summary of Cruz’s bill notes that it would require agents representing college athletes to register with at least one state and caps their compensation for negotiating Name, Image, and Likeness deals at 5% of a contract’s value. It bans the NCAA and its member institutions from limiting what student-athletes can make from such deals and establishes a reporting requirement for any deal worth more than $600.The bill would also bar colleges and NIL collectives from paying athletes in ways that undermine the revenue-sharing rules established by a 2025 federal court ruling in House v. NCAA. That groundbreaking case challenged the NCAA’s ban on direct athlete compensation on antitrust grounds and cleared the way for some former college athletes to share in up to $2.8 billion in back pay. The Athletic reported that NCAA institutions paid out more than $1.77 billion to athletes in the first year of that arrangement.And that’s where much of the conflict arises. Many critics of college athletics, including supporters of Cruz’s bill, point to the money flowing to college athletes and their ability to use the transfer portal to secure better financial deals as primary evidence that the NCAA has gone off the rails. But athletes’ newfound mobility and the agency that comes with it are long overdue, especially considering the way coaches and athletic directors have managed their careers to maximize their compensation.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/Qh_GVkEMkbY

According to the Knight-Newhouse College Athletics Database, total compensation to coaches in the NCAA Football Bowl Subdivision, the highest level of college football, was $1.6 billion in inflation-adjusted dollars in 2014, the year a judge ruled that college athletes could receive compensation for the use of their names, images and likenesses. Those payments have climbed in the years since.

Then or now, hardly anyone has begrudged college coaches for leveraging the rules and their own success to fatten their pockets by leaving one school to sign with the highest bidder. When it was only coaches and administrators who benefited, nobody in Congress thought a law limiting them to switching jobs only once was a good idea. But Cruz’s bill would do exactly that to college athletes and limit them to only one transfer. That provision alone — an attempt to limit athletes from maximizing their value in an emerging marketplace — should have been enough to make anyone who’s ever expressed praise for “free markets” in the halls of Congress to walk away. Instead, 77 senators voted for it. It’s not expected to fare as well in the House.

Public institutions cannot depend upon Black athletes to fill their stadiums, secure television contracts, attract donations, and build nationally recognized brands, then claim neutrality when the political rights of those athletes, their families, and their communities are under attack.NAACP PRESIDENT DERRICK JOHNSON

“Public institutions cannot depend upon Black athletes to fill their stadiums, secure television contracts, attract donations, and build nationally recognized brands, then claim neutrality when the political rights of those athletes, their families, and their communities are under attack,” Johnson wrote.Rather than view Cruz’s bill as a good-faith reform effort, the more cynical among us may see it as a midterm gift from politicians eager to help wealthy institutions and their benefactors bring college athletes to heel after those athletes finally won a modicum of control over their bodies and labor. Congress didn’t express concern with the size of checks, employee retention and mobility in college sports when coaches and athletic directors were exclusively benefiting. But they see a problem after athletes start cashing in big and moving.

The measure reportedly faces significant hurdles in the House, and lawmakers there who have signaled opposition to it are right. Rather than sending it to the president’s desk, they should rip it to shreds and burn it to ashes.

news.title: Odisha Reviews Anti-Drug Measures; 2.67 Lakh Students Reached Through Awareness Drives
news.text:
The 8th state-level Narcotics Coordination Centre (NCORD) review meeting, chaired by Garg, was held at Lok Seva Bhawan in Bhubaneswar. The meeting focused on reducing drug demand, strengthening de-addiction services, expanding public awareness and creating a drug-free environment in educational institutions.

Officials also discussed measures to prevent illegal cultivation of narcotic substances by promoting alternative crops and livelihood opportunities in vulnerable areas.

1,751 Awareness Programmes Reach 2.67 Lakh Students

The Special Task Force (STF) and NCORD presented details of expanded anti-drug awareness initiatives during the meeting.

As part of a special campaign conducted from August 16 to 31, as many as 1,751 awareness programmes were organised, reaching around 2,67,900 students.

The government also reviewed ongoing enforcement action against illegal drug trafficking. Six inter-state drug syndicates have been identified during state-level operations, with action initiated against those involved in the illegal trade.

Officials stressed that enforcement alone would not be sufficient to create a drug-free society. Awareness, rehabilitation services, youth participation, alternative livelihoods and community involvement were identified as equally important components of the strategy.

Focus on Alternative Livelihoods

The meeting placed particular emphasis on preventing illegal drug cultivation in vulnerable areas.

The Chief Secretary stressed the need for continuous awareness campaigns among communities in affected areas while ensuring that farmers have access to alternative crops and livelihood opportunities.

Officials discussed conducting awareness programmes and workshops at the village level to educate communities about alternative cultivation options and the legal consequences of illicit drug cultivation.

198 Villages Covered Under NDPS Awareness Drive

The government said extensive awareness activities on the NDPS Act are currently underway across 198 villages under 80 hotspot gram panchayats in 22 blocks.

Satellite imagery and remote-sensing technology are also being used to monitor areas where illegal cannabis cultivation may be taking place and to identify opportunities for alternative cultivation.

The meeting also discussed measures related to awareness campaigns, effective use of social media, perception management and systems to receive and respond to public feedback.

More Sports Activities for Youth

Garg stressed the need to keep young people engaged in sports and creative activities as part of efforts to prevent substance abuse.

She called for the preparation of annual sports calendars at the district level and more sports and creative programmes in vulnerable districts.

The Chief Secretary also advised authorities to work towards declaring educational institutions drug-free campuses.

Schools have been advised to form internal committees, maintain regular monitoring of students and increase awareness about the harmful effects of drugs.

The meeting also stressed the need for action to ensure that paan shops do not operate in the vicinity of educational institutions.

Joint Teams for Regular Checks and Raids

Garg directed departments to form joint teams to conduct regular inspections, surprise raids and monitoring operations to prevent the illegal trade and use of narcotic substances.

She also called for stronger district-level NCORD committees and more effective coordination among departments and enforcement agencies.

Particular emphasis was placed on regular monitoring and inter-departmental coordination to protect school and college students from the impact of drugs.

Foreign Nationals’ Cases Also Reviewed

The meeting also reviewed pending cases involving foreign nationals, including appeals against acquittal judgments and the implementation of the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025.

The government said comprehensive measures were being taken to prevent illegal drug cultivation in identified areas and strengthen coordination among agencies involved in drug-control operations.

Senior officials from the Home, Information and Public Relations departments, Odisha Police, STF, Narcotics Control Bureau, Odisha Maritime Board, Navy, CISF, Bhubaneswar airport, Railways and Paradip Port, among others, attended the meeting.

news.title: Fever 2026 timeline: How Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham and rivals likely changed the WNBA forever
news.text: The Indiana Fever's 2026 season may be studied by historians for decades to come. Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham, their supporting cast, rival players and neurotic fans and critics combined to form a perfect storm of cultural chaos. It pushed the WNBA to new heights in TV ratings and attendance, all while driving two sides of America further apart in a deepening cultural divide, sparking often-emotional debates on race and sexuality, day after day. WNBA COMMISSIONER CATHY ENGELBERT TO RETIRE AT END OF CALENDAR YEAR, ENDING CONTROVERSIAL TENURE The entire WNBA will be coming out of the season a completely different league than what it was going into 2026, as there will be a change in commissioner, all while two former NBA players are now declared for the 2027 draft. Here's how it all went down. April – The calm before the storm The Fever entered 2026 with championship expectations. Clark was preparing to return after injuries limited her to just 13 games last year, as Cunningham was returning from injury too. Kelsey Mitchell and Lexie Hull re-signed to reunite the core that carried to the brink of the 2025 Finals. The Fever also added veterans Monique Billings, Tyasha Harris and Myisha Hines-Allen and drafted South Carolina guard Raven Johnson with the No. 10 pick. Before training camp, Hull, who had become a fan-favorite in 2025, told Fox News Digital what it was like living inside the Clark-generated media spotlight that began in 2024. "The most challenging part is there's just so much scrutiny," Hull said. "People need to know that everyone's human. We're real people. I think when things get blown out of proportion, when things get really personal and there's personal attacks on people's character, I think that's where it gets over the line." Hull disputed the idea that opponents had necessarily become more physical with Clark, arguing that social media magnified every collision and missed call. But she acknowledged that the Fever’s massive following gave opponents extra motivation whenever Indiana came to town. The attention also came with an upside. Hull told Fox News Digital that seeing young fans arrive in Fever gear and aspire to play professional basketball had been "the most rewarding part" of the Clark era. After Indiana came within one victory of the 2025 WNBA Finals despite losing Clark and Cunningham to injuries, Hull declared the 2026 championship goal "very achievable." But they had no idea what laid ahead. Early May – Foreshadowing chaos Clark’s long-awaited regular-season return came in front of a sold-out Gainbridge Fieldhouse crowd on May 9. The opener pitted Clark against Dallas Wings guard Paige Bueckers, another former No. 1 overall pick whose arrival gave the league a second young superstar capable of drawing enormous national attention. The teams were called for a combined 53 fouls, disrupting a game that still came down to the final possession, as Clark missed a deep 3-pointer that could have forced overtime. Hours after the loss, Clark joined country music star Morgan Wallen for his signature concert walkout at Lucas Oil Stadium. The hometown crowd roared as Clark emerged alongside Wallen, but the appearance immediately dragged her back into the cultural and racial debates that had followed her since entering the WNBA. Critics condemned Clark for associating with Wallen, who was recorded using a racial slur in 2021 and later apologized. ESPN contributor Jayson Buford called the appearance "blatantly corny" and wrote that Clark was beloved "despite her proximity to the type of whiteness that is inherently scary." Other fans criticized Clark for celebrating at a concert only hours after missing a potential game-tying shot in Indiana’s loss. CAITLIN CLARK CALLS FOR FULL-TIME WNBA REFEREES AS OFFICIATING FAILURES MOUNT IN 2026 Others accused Clark’s critics of applying a double standard. Jemele Hill noted that Peyton Manning, Travis Kelce, Patrick Mahomes, Myles Garrett and Marshawn Lynch were among the prominent sports figures who had participated in Wallen’s concert entrances without generating comparable outrage. Cunningham, meanwhile, celebrated her teammate’s appearance in an Instagram post. Four days later, Clark picked up her first technical foul of the year during an 87-78 victory over the Los Angeles Sparks. After being called for an offensive foul late in the first half, Clark approached referee Jason Alabanza, clapped in his face and continued arguing as the teams headed toward their locker rooms. "I think the refs are doing a tremendous job," Clark told USA Network reporter Paris Lawson that night. "I deserved the technical they gave me. But it’s great for the game. They’re going to keep the hands off; they’re going to make the play be good. Obviously they called a lot of fouls tonight but it’s going to even out. So, you’ve got to give them credit. They’re doing the right thing." But coach Stephanie White criticized the referees after the game. "A lot of us spent a lot of time in the offseason on various committees trying to remedy this officiating thing," White said. "This felt a lot like last year to me. And that's not where we want it to be." On May 17, Cunningham came off the bench and scored 17 points in an 89-78 win over the Seattle Storm. But her most viral moment came after she blocked former Indiana University star Mackenzie Holmes and celebrated emphatically. When critics said she was doing too much over one regular-season block, Cunningham responded on social media. "HAHAHA ‘act like you’ve been there before’….. okay but the last I did this was against my 2 year old niece," Cunningham wrote. "LET ME LIVE!!!!" Late May to mid June – Tension rises The Fever’s championship expectations began to buckle after consecutive losses to Golden State and expansion Portland. During a 100-84 loss to the Fire on May 30, Clark scored only six points on 1-of-7 shooting and was seen arguing with White during a timeout, fueling online speculation about a rift between the superstar and her coach. Clark rejected suggestions of a fractured relationship when she spoke to reporters June 1. "First of all, two people being competitive. Two people that really want to win," Clark said. White added, "I think what happened in that moment is I was challenging a player. It’s coaching. It’s what it is. I don't often think it becomes an issue if you're watching it in men's sports most of the time." But Cunningham’s remarks the following day suggested the Fever still believed a serious internal conversation was necessary. "We had a team meeting Monday — a long meeting — and so hopefully we’ve kind of turned the page," Cunningham told reporters June 2. She estimated the meeting lasted between 90 minutes and two hours, began with the coaches and ended with the players speaking among themselves. She called the discussion "much needed." "We’re just too soft right now, and that’s not what our identity is, so we need to get away from that." The Fever briefly appeared to find their footing after the meeting. On June 8, Clark buried a deep 3-pointer with 1.2 seconds remaining to give Indiana a 78-76 victory over Washington Three days later, she produced 32 points and 10 assists in a 114-106 overtime win against Chicago. Clark received another technical foul late in Indiana’s June 13 victory over Connecticut after exchanging words with Saniya Rivers. Then came the renewal with Clark's rivalry against Angel Reese, who was now a part of the Atlanta Dream. The Fever then played consecutive games against Reese and the Dream in mid June. On June 18, Reese appeared to mock Clark for trying to draw a foul after the two made contact. Reese later caught Cunningham in the face with an elbow while battling for a rebound, although officials assessed only a common foul. Atlanta won 108-101. Two days later, Reese swiped at the ball in Clark’s hands after Clark was fouled, prompting the longtime rivals to exchange words. The brief confrontation quickly spread across social media as Atlanta won again, 113-96, as Clark was seen rolling her eyes while talking with White on the sideline. June 22-24 – The point and the punch The fuse was lit June 22. During the fourth quarter of Indiana’s first game against Phoenix, Clark and former Fever teammate DeWanna Bonner became entangled while fighting for position. Words were exchanged. Players converged and the officials ultimately assessed five technical fouls. Then Cunningham pointed right at Bonner. Standing several feet away from Bonner, Cunningham extended her arm, locked eyes with her former Phoenix teammate and silently pointed at her for approximately 22 seconds. The moment was so prolonged, so unusual and so perfectly suited for the internet that it instantly became one of the WNBA season’s defining images. Cunningham later explained that Bonner told her, "Don’t you point at me." That only made Cunningham want to continue. "And I was just kind of pointing, and she is like, ‘Don’t you point at me,’ and I was like, ‘Oh, shouldn’t have said that,’ and I didn’t say a word," Cunningham said on her podcast. Then came the rematch that changed everything. With 6:52 remaining in the second quarter June 24, Clark drove into the lane and fell onto her side after contact. As Clark and Phoenix players scrambled for the loose ball, Thomas dove toward the floor. Video showed Thomas appearing to press a closed fist directly into Clark's throat. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Thomas then rose and stepped over Clark as play continued. The referees called nothing. No personal foul. No technical foul. No flagrant review. The replay spread across social media, where fans dissected the contact frame by frame and once again accused WNBA officials of allowing opponents to take non-basketball shots at Clark without immediate consequences. Clark remained in the game initially but departed during the third quarter with a back injury and did not return. Phoenix escaped with a 111-109 victory. White unleashed one of the most blistering postgame attacks on WNBA officiating of the Clark era. "The fact that it was a no-call, it’s absolutely egregious and utterly disrespectful," White said. "We have a generational talent and a WNBA superstar who had two cheap shots right there that weren’t called," White said. "She is not called the same way as everybody else is called. The fist in the throat is crazy. It’s crazy. It’s dangerous." The officials had missed it in real time. The league office could not ignore it on replay. On June 25, the WNBA retroactively assessed Thomas a Flagrant-2 foul for a "non-basketball act," concluding that she had recklessly made contact with her fist to Clark’s throat area. Thomas received a one-game suspension and a $1,000 fine. It was the first suspension of her 13-year WNBA career. "Player safety should be paramount in our league," Fever president Kelly Krauskopf said in a statement. "We appreciate the WNBA’s review of last night’s incident and the action taken. Right now our focus is on Caitlin and our entire team as we prepare for Saturday." The season would never be just about basketball after that, and it was still only beginning. End of June to early July – Crisis mismanagement Thomas's punishment divided the public. Clark supporters argued one game was insufficient for an ejectable non-basketball act. Thomas defenders maintained that slow-motion replays and freeze frames made an accidental collision appear deliberate. Clark missed Indiana’s June 27 game against Los Angeles with a back injury. The Fever did not attribute the injury to Thomas’ contact, and Clark had already experienced back trouble earlier in the season. Meanwhile, Cunningham’s 22-second point became one of the year’s biggest sports memes. On June 30, the White House posted an edited video pairing Cunningham’s gesture with President Donald Trump pointing, transforming a moment of basketball trash talk into a national political symbol. That same day, Thomas said she and members of her family had received death threats and racial slurs following the incident. She also criticized Commissioner Cathy Engelbert for failing to defend the league’s players publicly. Engelbert responded by condemning the abuse. "We still have yet to hear anything from Cathy, it’s no surprise," Thomas said. "As usual, she remains silent, and that’s unfortunate when our lives are being threatened." Engelbert responded later that day. "The WNBA vehemently condemns any and all forms of hate," she said, adding that the threats and racial abuse described by Thomas were "completely unacceptable and not representative of the WNBA community." The statement came only after Thomas called out the commissioner, intensifying criticism that the league had been reactive throughout the controversy. Clark addressed the fallout July 3. She agreed that Thomas’ contact warranted a flagrant foul and said the league needed to improve its officiating and protection of players. But Clark also forcefully condemned the attacks directed at Thomas. "The harassment, the hate — none of that is OK," Clark said. Mid July – A whole new ball game Day after day, the temperature rose. And every big to medium name in sports media was getting their turn with the thermostat. On June 25, Boomer Esiason argued that Clark was denied respect because she was a "straight white basketball player" and should consider leaving the WNBA. Three days later, ESPN analyst Chiney Ogwumike said Clark could "embellish contact" and suggested the league reacted to the optics of a viral freeze-frame. On June 29, Emmanuel Acho declared that the WNBA would be "better off" without Clark because she had become more distraction than asset—even while crediting her with helping deliver charter flights, a lucrative media agreement and richer contracts. The stakes rose into politics, medicine and even the Olympics. On July 2, former Philadelphia 76ers orthopedic consultant Dr. Nicholas DiNubile gave a harrowing warning to Clark, telling Fox News Digital that as little as 10 to 20 pounds of pressure could damage the throat or larynx, while swelling or bleeding could rapidly obstruct an airway if she were to get hit in the throat again. The controversy inevitably reached the White House on July 6, when President Donald Trump said Clark had been "treated rather rough" and called the Thomas incident "a pretty bad event." Two days later, 11 Republican House members led by Rep. August Pfluger demanded answers from Engelbert about what they described as repeated hostility and violence against Clark. Their letter suggested investigations by the Justice Department, Labor Department or Equal Employment Opportunity Commission if discrimination or retaliation were creating a hostile workplace were on the table. The Fever said neither the organization nor Clark knew about or participated in the effort. Jemele Hill called the GOP intervention "f---ing ridiculous," while CNN’s Abby Phillip said Republican support for Clark appeared to exist "exclusively because she is White." Engelbert did little to regain control. On July 10, Dan Patrick said the commissioner canceled a scheduled interview on his show. Patrick said his staff had waited nearly two hours. Footage of Engelbert golfing nearby as he discussed the cancellation only made the optics worse. On July 16, eight Olympians representing the United States, Jamaica and Germany told Fox News Digital that they believed WNBA had failed to adequately protect Clark and called for the league to consistently enforce its rules. The group included gold medalists Nancy Hogshead and Donna de Varona. But the next night Clark reminded everyone why the entire country was arguing about her. While operating under a minutes restriction, Clark erupted for a career-high 45 points, 10 assists and four steals in less than 30 minutes as Indiana defeated Seattle 110-107. She became the first player in WNBA history to record at least 40 points and 10 assists in one game, while producing the highest-scoring performance ever by a point guard or Fever player. For one night, basketball reclaimed the story. But it wouldn't last. Late July – All-Stars and activism On July 21, an ESPN profile revealed the now-famous or infamous quote from Cunningham: "I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men." The Fever's second biggest star became a folk hero for the "Save Women's Sports" movement. The quote split instantly along familiar political lines. Cunningham refused to retreat when reporters questioned her July 22. "I said what I said. I think it’s kind of common sense," she said. "I think it’s really important to protect children, and that’s little girls who are also involved in that category." Clark, meanwhile, wasn't done being used as a martyr to discuss racism. USA Today columnist Nancy Armour argued that Clark’s alleged flopping and berating of officials fueled racist harassment and placed Black and queer players in danger. Armour invoked the murder of Emmett Till while connecting the controversy to America’s history of White women portraying Black people as threats. After intense backlash, Armour apologized for what she called an "inartful comparison." Clark appeared to push back on the cultural narratives during All-Star weekend, accusing the media of creating a "false characterization" of her and making accusations about her character without knowing her. "It’s emotionally exhausting, it’s draining, it makes your shoulders tense, because you know, people don’t want to talk about the basketball," Clark said. "They want to stir it up and make it something else." Former President Barack Obama then surprised the All-Stars at practice and encouraged Clark not to let the surrounding "nonsense" destroy her joy for basketball. But a new storm was waiting for the Fever once All-Star weekend was over. July 28-29 – The birth of 'Sophie Night' The Fever's first game after the All-Star break was in Seattle against the Storm. That night, Outside Climate Pledge Arena, Cunningham’s defense of female-only sports prompted banners, balloons, a life-size cardboard cutout and a billboard truck declaring, "Sophie supports women & girls! Save women’s sports." The rally was organized by independent journalist and podcast host Brandi Kruse, women’s-rights advocate Amy E. Sousa — known online as "Known Heretic" — and the group Women Are Real. The rally promoted Washington Initiative 638, which would prohibit students defined as biologically male from competing in certain female-only K-12 sports and require medical verification of biological sex. Supporters carried signs reading "Thank you Sophie," "I said what I said" and "With love is truth." Counterprotesters arrived with LGBTQ flags and signs supporting transgender inclusion. The divide continued inside. the arena Storm center Stefanie Dolson entered the arena wearing a "Trans rights are human rights" shirt. Cunningham was booed when she checked into the game and again when she attempted her first free throws. Then during the game, two teenage girls wearing XX-XY Athletics shirts held a sign reading, "Thank you Sophie for speaking up for girls." One of them was Washington high school runner Ahnaleigh Wilson, who said she had competed against a transgender athlete several times and attended her first WNBA game because Cunningham’s remarks made her feel supported. The girls alleged Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton approached them and called them "f---ing insane." One day later, the story had shaken the nation, erupting on social media and across mainstream news. The Storm was forced to acknowledge the incident and apologized, before the WNBA later fined Keaton and suspended her from Seattle’s next five home games. And Cunningham was quick to weigh in on the matter herself. Cunningham reposted Fox News Digital’s report on X about Keaton’s punishment, writing, "I truly believe there is a safe space and love for EVERYBODY," Cunningham wrote. "You can disagree and still be kind." She praised the teenagers for defending their beliefs, promised to send them gifts and called Keaton’s alleged conduct "truly embarrassing." The incident set the WNBA's drama on a track from a hot topic in sports media into the spotlight of a one-month national obsession. July 31- August 28 – The month of mayhem The "Save Women's Sports" movement had found its road map in the Fever’s upcoming schedule after the Storm game. The next stop was just down the West coast in Portland. As the second Cunningham rally raged outside the Moda Center, once again pitting women's sports advocates against pro-trans counter-protesters, WNBA coaches faced consequential questioning inside. An OutKick reporter pressed both White and Fire coach Alex Sarama on their stances on whether biological males should be allowed to compete in women's sports. Neither coach gave a clear yes or no answer, and their responses frustrated all sides on social media. White's response in particular, as the coach of Clark and Cunningham, drew national backlash all while her team was playing the game that night. "I don't think I'm educated enough," White said, adding "I never believe exclusion is the answer." The answer drew prominent voices across social media, on both sides of the aisle, into the debate that had suddenly gripped the WNBA. And that grip only tightened in the following weeks. The first use of the term "Sophie Night" appeared in an OutKick article previewing the third rally that was set to take place in Minnesota for the Fever's Aug. 2 game against the Lynx. The name stuck. On Aug. 2, Jennifer Sey, Riley Gaines and Michele Tafoya joined women’s sports advocates outside Target Center, where OutKick documented counterprotesters shouting slurs and security intervening during a physical confrontation. College softball player Kendall Kotzmacher later told Fox News Digital that one protester said she "should’ve been aborted." Inside, Lynx coach Cheryl Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" shirt, while Gaines alleged an arena employee tried to make her lower a sign that read, "Sophie, thank you — a girl mom." Gaines refused and later posed with Cunningham holding the sign. On the sidelines, Cunningham said Reeve approached her for a face-to-face conversation in which both shared their perspectives and "left with love and respect." Clark, meanwhile, was finally pulled into the debate. She declined to take a side, saying the issue was for "leagues and governing bodies" to resolve with their athletes and that Indiana’s focus was basketball. Then came the sleeping giants. On Aug. 7, former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White announced they intended to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft while identifying as women, openly challenging a collective bargaining agreement that limited eligibility to "players who are women" but did not further define the term. White first revealed his plan exclusively to OutKick. In response the WNBPA said transgender people should not be subjected to "hate, abuse and demonization" and declared that players would not be used as "political pawns." Commissioner Cathy Engelbert called the subject "complex and nuanced" in a memo to teams and promised listening sessions and additional discussions. Then Aug. 8 deteriorated whatever restraint remained. As a fourth Cunningham rally unfolded outside Chicago’s United Center, Sky guard DiJonai Carrington struck Cunningham across the face and neck as she drove toward the basket. Carrington received a flagrant-2 foul and was ejected, then posted "WHITE PRIVILEGE" and tagged the Fever. Carrington did not explain what the post meant or accuse Cunningham by name. There was also no evidence the foul was motivated by Cunningham’s position on transgender athletes. But Cunningham called the contact intentional and accused Carrington of seeking attention. "This has nothing to do with race," Cunningham said. "There’s no reason even to play that card." The fallout became nearly as combustible as the incident. Sports Illustrated changed a headline that initially described the hit as Cunningham receiving a "bitter taste of karma," while ESPN’s broadcast did not address Carrington’s "White privilege" post. The WNBA also imposed no additional discipline on Carrington, who was allowed to play in the Sky's next game. White also faced initial criticism after saying she did not believe Carrington intentionally targeted Cunningham’s neck, even as she agreed with the ejection. Indiana Lt. Gov. Micah Beckwith publicly called for her firing. After reviewing the replay, White called the hit "egregious." On Aug. 11, she delivered a prepared defense of her players and staff, denounced the "hate," "fearmongering" and "divisiveness" surrounding the league and concluded, "Everybody else can go to hell." Some Fever fans booed her that night. Clark said hearing it made her "a little sick," while Cunningham publicly stood behind her coach. The next day, a league task force of team presidents and general managers discussed transgender eligibility but established no new standard. The WNBA said there were "no immediate eligibility matters" and condemned "bad-faith efforts" to demean or marginalize others. But the rallies kept spreading. At an Aug. 16 game in Atlanta, WNBA security ordered a mother and her 17-year-old daughter to cover their XX-XY shirts or leave. OutKick later learned that security also made a fan cover a "Protect Trans Kids" shirt. The league acknowledged the intervention "should not have happened," while the Dream said its personnel were not responsible. The game itself was one of the best contests of the regular season, as Clark and Cunningham escaped Atlanta with an overtime victory, avenging their earlier losses to Reese and the Dream earlier in the season. Clark was even seen laughing after Reese missed the game-winning layup. Two days later, Canadian powerlifting champion April Hutchinson led the seventh Cunningham rally and the first outside the United States in Toronto, where a billboard truck was told by police it had to shut down its message in support of protecting women's sports. Aug. 20, ahead of the Fever's game against the Wings in Dallas, the eighth "Sophie Night" had attracted Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who attended with his daughter in matching XX-XY shirts. Paxton told OutKick that he was monitoring the treatment of Cunningham’s supporters but announced no formal action. New York delivered the largest confrontation yet Aug. 22. Dueling crowds gathered behind police barriers outside Barclays Center ahead of the Fever's game against the liberty, where an OutKick photographer alleged his glasses were taken and officers escorted an OutKick reporter from a crowd of pro-trans protesters for his safety. Inside, the Liberty displayed three paid messages welcoming transgender fans. But Fox News Digital exclusively reported that the team had refunded lesbian hip-hop artist Julie Potter after attempting to rewrite her message: "Thank you Jennifer Sey! XX-XY Athletics will Save the Day!!" The circus reached its August climax one day later in Chicago. Carrington had teased the rematch by posting "8/23." But former NBA player Freedom stole the spectacle. Wearing a shirt defining a woman as an "adult human female," he attended the rally and sat courtside before becoming embroiled in a shouting match with Sky guard Natasha Cloud. Freedom said Cloud confronted him after he celebrated a Cunningham basket, alleging shouting at him "she's not going to sleep with you." Sky ownership said Freedom became a potential threat when he stood and stepped toward the court during the interaction with Cloud, as Security removed him, and Sky principal owner Michael Alter subsequently barred him from future home games. Alter told OutKick in an exclusive interview that some conduct does not warrant a warning, using firing a gun at someone as an "extreme example." Freedom denied threatening anyone and threatened legal action while speaking to OutKick later that day. Freedom made good on his promise of legal action just weeks later. But the spectacle ultimately produced the WNBA’s largest regular-season television audience in 29 years. On Aug. 24, unnamed league sources reportedly said Freedom and White were ineligible for the draft and called their declarations publicity stunts. The league, however, did not publicly identify the standard used to reach that conclusion. Freedom's stunt also seemingly drew mimicry from White. Four days later, White arrived at a Fever home game wearing a long blonde wig and introduced himself to OutKick as "Queen Roysha." Fans lined up for photographs. Gaines was also in the building that night, and her adversary and Olympic legend Simone Biles was the team's guest of honor for that game. Still, the guest that fans in the arena or on social media had the most interest in that night was White. In less than a month, Cunningham’s comments had spawned a traveling protest movement, dueling demonstrations, accusations of censorship and racism, a league task force, two former NBA players’ draft campaigns and a courtside confrontation that ended with one of them banned from an arena. The Fever were no longer merely a basketball team. They had become a traveling national referendum for a divided nation. Aug. 31-Sept. 13 – A World Cup ceasefire The WNBA took a break from the chaos right at its peak. The league paused for two weeks as Clark, Reese and Paige Bueckers joined Team USA for the FIBA Women’s World Cup in Berlin. No partnership carried more intrigue than Clark and Reese. The two stars both accepted reserve roles, frequently entered games together and were seen laughing and talking on the bench. Their complementary styles also produced some of Team USA’s most electric stretches. "We just continue to build chemistry because we know we’re going to be USA teammates for a while," Reese said after their best performance together in the quarterfinals. The Americans completed an undefeated run by defeating France on Sept. 13, capturing their fifth consecutive World Cup championship. Clark and Reese sat beside each other throughout the final round and connected on pivotal plays during the title game. Afterward, OutKick asked Clark whether she and Reese were friends now. "We’ve always been friends," Clark responded while wagging her finger. "Don’t try to do that. Don’t try to do that." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The exchange immediately went viral, becoming the subject of another heated media debate over whether the Clark-Reese rivalry was real, exaggerated or manufactured entirely by the press. Mid September to October – Out with a bang After the World Cup break dampened the discourse around women's sports, Clark and Cunningham returned to WNBA action Sept. 18, and quietly finished out the regular season with two wins and two losses. The Fever returned to Minnesota on Sept. 24 for their regular-season finale, where the final "Sophie Night" rally of the year unfolded outside Target Center. An opposing protester told Cunningham supporters through a bullhorn that they "should have been aborted," while another repeatedly called the XX-XY Athletics organization a "hate group." Inside, Minnesota routed Indiana 86-66. Clark scored a career-low two points, Aliyah Boston suffered a lower-leg injury and Tyasha Harris had to be carried from the floor. The Fever finished 28-16, fell to the No. 6 seed and drew the defending champion Las Vegas Aces. Aces star and WNBA legend A'ja Wilson immediately delivered a reality check. She overwhelmed Indiana with 38 points and 16 rebounds in a 102-85 Game 1 rout. Las Vegas led by as many as 27. Facing elimination Sept. 29, Clark answered with one of the greatest playoff performances in league history. She became the first WNBA player to record a points-assists double-double before halftime of a playoff game and finished with 27 points, 15 assists and seven rebounds in Indiana’s 99-89 victory. A second-quarter technical foul only ignited her, as the Fever responded with a 24-6 run. Clark eventually fouled out with 2:45 remaining, but she had already forced the series back to Las Vegas. Then the basketball game became something else. Late in the fourth quarter, Wilson and Cunningham became tangled during a physical play. A male spectator behind the basket stood and pointed toward Wilson, prompting her to move toward him before teammates and officials intervened. Wilson received a technical foul, while the spectator was temporarily escorted from his seat and later allowed to return. A witness told OutKick that the man had only shouted, "It’s on you!" Wilson offered a different perspective, saying the man had stepped toward her and that his gesture and tone were "unacceptable." Fever security interviewed the fan and witnesses and found no Fan Code of Conduct violation. The WNBA later reached the same conclusion. The league also determined Wilson had remained in a designated "player escape lane," not entered the stands, explaining why she was not automatically ejected or suspended. Enes Kanter Freedom, who had been removed and later banned from Chicago Sky games after his own courtside confrontation, called it a double standard and told OutKick Wilson should have been suspended. Cunningham naturally poured gasoline on it. The next morning, she posted a TikTok marveling at the "comeback year for the point," invoking both the Wilson incident and her own viral finger-pointing confrontation with DeWanna Bonner earlier in the season. Wilson got the final response. Game 3 opened in open hostility. Just over three minutes into the winner-take-all contest, former Fever player Brianna Turner worked her way into Indiana’s on-court huddle. Clark shoved her out. Both players received technical fouls. Early in the second quarter, Turner appeared to hook Hull’s arm and pull her to the floor. Officials called the foul on Hull. White, Hull and the Fever bench pleaded for a timeout and challenge, but the officials allowed Las Vegas to proceed with a free throw, closing Indiana’s opportunity for review. The Fever bench received another technical foul amid the confusion. Indiana still twice pulled within two points during the fourth quarter. Then, with the Fever trailing 82-77 and 3:16 remaining, Jewell Loyd inadvertently caught Clark in the mouth with an elbow while battling for a rebound. There was no whistle and no review. Clark briefly left the court with blood pouring from her mouth. When she returned, she pulled down her lip and showed the damage to an official. The Aces attempted 35 free throws to Indiana’s 20 in Game 3 and held an 89-58 advantage across the series, despite the Fever taking twice as many shots in the restricted area. White called it a "game of the margins" and noted the disparity after the game. "Hmm, interesting," Clark interjected. But the officials were not the entire story. Wilson was. She scored 36 points with 10 rebounds, while Clark and Mitchell combined to shoot 13-of-41. Las Vegas earned a 94-83 victory and eliminated Indiana for the second consecutive season. The questionable calls supplied one final controversy, but Wilson supplied the decisive answer. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER The Aces left with the series. Clark left Las Vegas with blood in her mouth. Now, as the Fever and the WNBA as a whole will look toward 2027 with questions abound, as to whether Cunningham will be returning to the team, and what the new commissioner will mean for the league's culture and Clark's presence.
news.summary: Caitlin Clark, Sophie Cunningham and the Indiana Fever sparked a cultural firestorm that pushed the WNBA into a national debate over race and gender.

news.text: p>This week on Hafta, Abhinandan Sekhri and Rinchen Norbu are joined by Supreme Court lawyers Neha Rathi and Shahrukh Alam, along with The News Minute’s executive editor Sudipto Mondal, to discuss the Supreme Court’s handling of the special intensive revision (SIR) of the voter roll and what it says about the state of India’s judiciary.The discussion begins with the Supreme Court declining to advance the hearing of a plea involving more than 18,000 appeals against the deletion of names from West Bengal’s voter rolls ahead of by-elections in Nandigram and Rejinagar. According to Bar and Bench, the Chief Justice of India said, “These are only by-elections, that’s all.” The panel discusses whether the apex court has become the destination for matters that should ordinarily be handled by lower courts, and whether the judiciary is taking the right to vote seriously enough.Neha, who was one of the petitioners challenging discrepancies in the SIR, explains why the matter reached the Supreme Court and argues that the scale of pending cases has made the situation particularly difficult. Shahrukh questions the latitude courts continue to extend to the state, arguing that “the state is given far more leeway” than citizens. The conversation also turns to the larger question of institutional faith, with Rinchen citing recent CSDS-Lokniti survey data showing a decline in public trust in the Election Commission.The panel then debates whether the judiciary’s problems are merely about individual benches or reflect deeper structural issues. Sudipto argues that the composition and social background of the judiciary need greater scrutiny.The discussion then shifts to student politics and whether Indian universities are becoming increasingly insulated from political activity. For this segment, Abha Dev Habib, professor at Delhi University’s Miranda House and Joint Secretary of the Democratic Teachers’ Front, joins the conversation.Abha argues that politics is an integral part of education, while distinguishing it from violence on campuses. news.title: D.C. Memo: Reining in college sports ‘chaos’
news.text:
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Senate approved a bill to regulate college sports this week that was a year in the making.

The Protect College Sports Act was approved on a lopsided 77-22 vote, with both Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith supportive of the legislation.

Supporters of the legislation say it is needed to sort out the “chaos” in college sports.

But there is still controversy over the bill, with critics saying it would give the NCAA more power over players and cap the compensation that student athletes could earn. 

The University of Minnesota joined all Big Ten schools in supporting the bill.

The bill would grant the NCAA and athletic conferences an antitrust exemption that would allow the NCAA to restore its five-year eligibility rule and transfer limits.

The legislation would also cap agent fees at 5% and protect athletic scholarships from being revoked due to injury, illness or performance.

It would also establish a national, federal standard for an athlete’s right to earn compensation for their name, image and likeness (NIL), replacing a patchwork of state laws on compensation.

The bill would also create a new $22.5 million fund for schools to retain student athletes, allowing it to grow to $27.5 million if schools invest in NIL for women’s and Olympic sports.

Yet opponents of the bill called it a long-term threat to college athletics and said it would cap the earnings and organizing potential of college athletes and create a permanent imbalance of power between college athletes and athletic conferences.

They also say the antitrust exception would restrain lawsuits and legal challenges the NCAA has faced in recent years.

And they say the bill was drafted without any meaningful input from the student-athletes themselves.

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., who has fought for compensation of student- athletes, pushed back against claims that college sports is in “crisis” and in need of the bill’s new regulations.

“I know that there’s more people than ever showing up to these games and watching the games,” Murphy said in a statement. “The Big 10 just signed a $13 billion contract to broadcast its games.”

He also said the revenue of the NCAA is at an all-time high and the Southeastern Conference (SEC) and Big 10 are both making over $1 billion.

Besides the 22 senators who voted against the bill — most of them Democrats — the Protect College Sports Act is opposed by the Congressional Black Caucus, the NAACP and the AFL-CIO.

The debate over the bill now moves to the House, where its future is uncertain. The House won’t return to work until after November’s midterm election, so any opportunity to consider the bill would come in a lame-duck session of Congress. 

Klobuchar breaks from party on data center vote

President Donald Trump and executives of the nation’s major tech companies signed an agreement this week to voluntarily police their AI systems, agreeing to work with “independent auditors” to assess whether AI systems are working as they were designed to.

But many Americans may not think that’s not enough of a safeguard.

A Quinnipiac poll released this week found that 73% of Americans are either very concerned (38%) or somewhat concerned (35%) that future AI systems could potentially threaten human survival.

Seventy-four percent of poll respondents said they have either not so much trust (29%) or none at all (45%) in the leaders of AI companies.

Meanwhile, Congress struggled this week to place regulations on the data centers that would power AI systems.

Most Senate Democrats argued that a bill called the Ratepayer Protection Act that’s aimed at protecting Americans from escalating energy costs does not go far enough.

The bill would require — but not mandate — that states consider a framework that would ensure that data centers pay for all energy costs and grid updates.

Senate Minority leader Charles Schumer, D-N.Y., who led the opposition, said “a guardrail without teeth isn’t a guardrail.”

The legislation was approved several weeks ago by an overwhelming margin, 417 -3, in the U.S. House.

But it failed to win the 60 votes needed to advance in the U.S. Senate, even as four Democrats, including Klobuchar, broke from their party to vote to move the bill forward.

Klobuchar admitted the bill “would be just a start and it would not fix everything.”

“My focus is on making sure that Minnesotans — not Big Tech — have the final say on data centers, and that involves strong state standards and local control,” she said in an emailed statement. “Minnesotans don’t want a data center in their community, I don’t want it there either.”

Klobuchar, who is running for governor, also said she supports banning nondisclosure agreements for data centers. She also said, “I will make sure that Minnesotans aren’t getting hosed on their electric bills and that our state’s water is protected.” 

Meanwhile, Minnesota’s other Democratic senator, Tina Smith, voted to block the bill.

Democratic opposition to the bill is thought to have been driven, at least in part, by efforts to avoid bolstering the reelection of the bill’s sponsor, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is in a tough race for reelection against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown.

Klobuchar has the brainiest staffers

Members of Congress are ranked on many things, including their voting record, attendance and how much campaign cash they raise.

LegiStorm also ranked them by how much education they, and their staffers have.

It found that Sen. Amy Klobuchar has the most educated staffers, followed by Sen. Tina Smith.

That should not be surprising since senators have a larger budget to hire staff and more committee work that requires able researchers and experts in a variety of issues.

On the House side, Rep. Angie Craig, D-2nd District, had the most educated staffers, according to LegiStorm, even as the congresswoman in 2023 announced that a college requirement was not needed to work in her Washington, D.C., or district offices.

“Nobody’s career trajectory should be predetermined by a piece of paper — it should be determined by their work ethic, experience and ability to do the job in front of them,” Craig said at the time.

The office with the least educated staffers was Rep. Brad Finstad, R-1st District.

Finstad’s office did not return a request for comment.

Staff education levels can vary because some offices have more entry level staffers than others, depressing overall education levels.

LegiStorm ranked the education level of all House and Senate offices by considering the level of education — including professional degrees, associate degrees, bachelor’s degrees and post-graduate degrees — and weighing the institutions that granted those degrees.

National universities — schools that offer a full range of undergraduate (bachelor’s) majors, as well as master’s and doctoral degrees — are weighed more heavily than regional universities or liberal arts colleges.

LegiStorm also ranked the education level of all members of Congress.

In Minnesota’s delegation, Rep. Kelly Morrison, D-3rd District — who attended Yale as an undergrad and Boston University for her graduate studies and received a medical degree from Case Western Reserve University — is the most educated.

Klobuchar, who attended Yale and the University of Chicago Law School, came in a close second.

In other news:

▪️Matthew Blake has an in-depth profile of Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth that explains how she climbed the ranks of power. The first installment is here and the second is here.

▪️Just before St. Paul’s Central Senior High was to begin its fall sports season, it was discovered that rubber pellets under the artificial turf on its playing field had turned into clumps, causing many problems. Metro reporter Trevor Mitchell has a story about how this happened and what the school is doing about it.

▪️There’s evidence that the race for U.S. Senate between Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and former sportscaster Michele Tafoya has tightened and the result of the contest will be determined by which candidate prevails in the attacks on her opponent. 

▪️Greater Minnesota reporter Brian Arola explains why 17 state legislative races are already in the DFL column as contests for control of the Legislature are bitterly fought in other places. 

Please keep your comments, and any questions, coming. I’ll try my best to respond. I can be reached at aradelat@minnpost.com.

news.title: Kalshi Is Lobbying States to Fight Off Regulations for Prediction Markets
news.text:
As prediction markets have exploded in popularity over the past two years, they have also become increasingly controversial – setting off a lobbying-fueled power struggle for regulation of the platforms. 

Amid allegations of insider trading, bets on military operations, and deceptive marketing practices, some states are seeking to sue or ban prediction markets. But the federal government has taken an unusual role in the legal battle, with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission suing states that seek to enforce their gambling laws against prediction-market platforms.

Prediction market companies contend they are offering financial transactions known as swaps – which are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, a federal agency – while many states argue they are gambling operations, akin to sportsbooks and casinos. Gambling is regulated by the states. 

Several lawsuits addressing whether state law applies to prediction markets have advanced to federal courts, but because judges have split on their rulings, the question is still unsettled and moving towards the Supreme Court. 

Although market leader Kalshi argues it should be regulated at the federal level, the company’s lobbying and spending demonstrates a push to gain state-level influence – especially in the states spearheading regulation. 

So far in 2026, Kalshi, its competitor Polymarket and the Coalition for Prediction Markets have spent at least $3 million on lobbying and campaign contributions across the federal and state levels.

Kalshi Directs Political Spending to Governors and State AGs

State attorneys general are leading the regulatory fight against prediction markets – and the majority are united in the opinion that CFTC regulation should not preempt state gambling laws. In July, a coalition of 44 state AGs signed onto a letter to the CFTC arguing that prediction markets are a “new form of casino.” 

But just as attorneys general and prediction markets appear to be battling each other, Kalshi is pouring hundreds of thousands of dollars into the two major political organizations dedicated to electing and supporting AGs. 

According to IRS filings reviewed by OpenSecrets, in the first half of 2026, Kalshi gave $147,500 to the Republican Attorneys General Association and $170,000 to the Democratic Attorneys General Association. 

Kalshi has also donated directly to some attorneys general – including the super PAC supporting Ken Paxton’s run for Senate in Texas and the campaigns of Vermont’s Charity Clark, Oregon’s Dan Rayfield and Florida’s James Utheimer. In response to the contributions, Rayfield and Clark told local news outlets they are not influenced by political donations. A spokesperson for Paxton’s super PAC told Politico that Paxton “has fought at every turn to hold big corporations accountable.”

The New York Times reported in August that Donald Trump Jr., who serves as a strategic advisor to Kalshi and Polymarket, told Republican state AGs not to fight prediction markets. Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm is invested in Polymarket and he has an equity stake in Kalshi.

The head of Kalshi’s state relations, Blake Bee, was previously director of the National Association of Attorneys General’s Center for Leadership Development, where he worked directly with state attorneys general. 

Kalshi also donated $100,000 to the Republican Governors Association and $150,000 to the Democratic Governors Association in the first half of 2026. 

“Like many U.S. regulated companies, we support candidates on both sides of the aisle,” Dani Lever, a spokesperson for Kalshi, wrote in a statement to OpenSecrets.

Kalshi Hires Dozens of New Lobbyists, Focusing on California and New York

Kalshi has ramped up state-level lobbying in the past several months. As of September, the company has at least one registered lobbyist in 41 states, nearly all of them brought on board since April.

Kalshi appears to be spending the most on lobbying in California and New York, though many states do not require financial disclosure by lobbyists. 

In California, Kalshi spent $62,000 on lobbying in the first half of 2026. Disclosure reports reviewed by OpenSecrets show that Kalshi is lobbying on three assembly bills and the “Attorney General’s and Governor’s offices re: prediction markets.” 

Kalshi’s California lobbying has so far been handled by Redwood Public Affairs. Redwood’s co-founder and principal was formerly the legislative director and chief of staff for state Attorney General Rob Bonta. On Aug. 12, Kalshi registered another California-based firm, the Weideman Group, to begin lobbying. 

In New York, Kalshi recently reported that it would increase its payment to lobbyists at Brown & Weinraub Advisors from $10,000 monthly to $25,000 monthly to work on legislation relating to prediction markets. 

Kalshi is spreading its Empire State work around, also committing to pay $25,000 monthly to the Mirram Group in a contract running until July 2027. Additionally, Kalshi has registered Blake Bee as its in-house lobbyist in New York. Bee will lobby the office of the governor and the state assembly through December 2026, according to the registration. 

Between its payments to both lobbying groups and Bee, Kalshi is currently projected to spend over $400,000 on lobbying in New York through July 2027. 

Through its state-level lobbying efforts, Kalshi may be positioned to deal with a flood of new laws if the Supreme Court rules that prediction markets should be regulated by the states as gambling. 

“Most state gambling laws are designed for sporting events, poker, casino games, but they mostly clearly cover gambling in whatever form or packaging,” said Benjamin Schriffin, director of securities policy at Better Markets, a nonprofit that advocates for financial reform. “I don’t think anybody ever conceived of having to pass a law that’s going to prevent people who are watching ‘Survivor ‘at home on a Wednesday night from betting on who’s going to win. So you could see states thinking, ‘We need to clarify our gambling laws for all these new ways that people have now found to gamble on prediction markets.’”

Polymarket has not yet registered any lobbyists at the state level. 

Kalshi Continues Federal Lobbying, Spending Nearly $1 Million in the First Half of 2026

As it expands its state presence, Kalshi is also continuing its federal lobbying by spending nearly $1 million through June 30. 

In January, Kalshi opened a Washington, D.C., office headed by John Bivona, who served on the Joe Biden’s presidential campaign and as the Department of Homeland Security’s White House liaison during the Biden administration. 

In addition to its in-house federal lobbying team, Kalshi has hired six outside firms. Kalshi relies most on Miller Strategies, which it has paid $240,000 during the first half of 2026. Miller Strategies is headed by Jeff Miller, who served as finance chair on President Donald Trump’s second inaugural committee and has grown his shop into the fifth highest-grossing lobbying firm in the first half of 2026.

Kalshi has also reported $120,000 in lobbying expenses to Lincoln Policy Group, founded by former Sen. Blanche Lincoln (D-Ark.). While in the Senate, Lincoln chaired the Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee – the CFTC’s authorizing committee.

As a lobbyist for Kalshi, Lincoln is now arguing directly against stances she took as chair. In 2010, Lincoln said the CFTC should be empowered to “prevent derivatives contracts that are contrary to the public interest because they exist predominantly to enable gambling through supposed ‘event contracts.’” In 2025, Lincoln submitted a public letter to the CFTC arguing that Kalshi should be permitted to offer sports bets in all states.

Kalshi has disclosed lobbying on three Senate bills – the Prediction Market Act, which would create stronger federal regulations on events contracts, the Protect College Sports Act and the National Defense Authorization Act. 

The Protect College Sports Act would create federal rules around athlete payment, transfers and conference alignment. Although lobbying disclosures do not specify Kalshi’s stance in its lobbying, the NCAA, which supports the bill, has previously stated its “vehement opposition” to prediction market contracts related to college sports. The Senate passed the bill on Monday and it now awaits action in the House of Representatives.

Kalshi’s lobbying on the NDAA is likely related to sections 1081, 1082, and 1083, which would ban “covered transactions” involving prediction market contracts, prevent Department of Defense personnel from trading on prediction markets, and ban all bets regarding military operations.

In addition to those three bills, Kalshi’s lobbying disclosures also reveal its focus on the CFTC, the Executive Office of the President, the Securities & Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress. 

The director of the CFTC has been explicitly pro-prediction market, both through public statements and the commission’s legal action against states attempting to regulate the platforms.

Brad Lipton, director of the Roosevelt Institute’s corporate power and financial regulation program, said the CFTC suing states is “unprecedented.”

“They’re being super aggressive, and it’s sort of a head scratcher as to why they’re being so aggressive,” Lipton said. “It’s because they’re so committed to helping out prediction markets, is really the only explanation.”

Beyond its corporate spending, Kalshi’s co-founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara have donated to federal political campaigns and political action committees. Mansour and Lopes Lara have collectively given about $1 million to both Democratic and Republican recipients this cycle, according to FEC filings. 

Polymarket has spent $180,000 on federal lobbying in 2026, hiring Advocus Partners. Advocus is a collaborative advocacy group whose members include BGR Group, one of the leading lobbying firms. Polymarket’s lobbyists include Keaghan Ames, a former senior policy advisor at the CFTC.

Coalition for Prediction Markets Brings in Other Players

In December 2025, Kalshi joined Robinhood, Coinbase, Crypto.com and Underdog – which all offer exchange betting in their apps – to launch the Coalition for Prediction Markets. Polymarket is not a member.

The coalition’s bipartisan leadership includes a pair of former House members. President Sean Patrick Maloney represented New York as a Democrat before serving in the Biden administration, and senior adviser Patrick McHenry was briefly the acting speaker of the House while he represented North Carolina as a Republican.

In July, the coalition named former CFTC Commissioner Brian Quintenz as a senior advisor and has brought on a pair of lobbying firms to work at the federal level. As of its June 30, the coalition had paid $100,000 to four Invariant lobbyists and registered two Determinant lobbyists. 

The coalition has also spent $50,000 lobbying in California through Redwood Public Affairs, the same lobbying firm used by Kalshi. 

The coalition’s crypto members are some of the biggest political spenders in the current election cycle. Crypto.com’s parent company, Foris Dax, is the largest donor to MAGA Inc., the main super PAC supporting President Donald Trump. Coinbase is the 10th largest political donor in this election cycle. 

The coalition follows a pattern of unified advocacy seen in other lines of business, much like that of the sports betting and gambling industry – which has spent millions on lobbying and industry-specific super PACs this year. 

Lipton said the current battle for regulatory control of prediction markets is an “existential question” for the platforms, likely motivating their attempts to increase their political influence.

“It’s not at all clear to me that their business model can compete if they are going to comply with state law,” Lipton said. “They’re really trying to create a situation, I think, where they have enough political power to overcome the legal deficiencies in their arguments.”

news.summary: Prediction market companies say they offer regulated financial swaps. Many states argue they are gambling operations.

news.title: College football playoff expansion is nothing more than a desperate financial bailout disguised as progress
news.text: Coming out of their meetings this week at Big Ten headquarters, the College Football Playoff committee is now formally waiting to see what ESPN is willing to offer for an expansion from 12 teams to 24. Only two years into this newer format, we're already pressing the issue of whether a quick jump is needed to suffice those who are struggling during these new times in college athletics where money seems to be the biggest conundrum. Now, with a straight face, those in favor of expanding the playoff want you to think it's anything other than a money grab during an era in which schools are having to find different ways to raise capitol. INSIDE THE FIGHT: NIL ARMS RACE FUELING NEW PUSH FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF EXPANSION No, this is not affecting some of the more prestigious schools in college athletics, who essentially print money in the bowels of their athletic department buildings. But, for those schools who are working overtime to create additional sources of income to pay for stadium renovations, house-settlement payouts, expensive contracts and who are also being dragged through the mud by bad television deals, the time has come to make a trip back to the bank teller in order to take out more funds. I guess we can call it an additional line of credit, or a hardship withdrawal. The formal offers for CFP expansion are going to cause a rift Right now, with the 30-day negotiating window coming to a close over the next week, ESPN is putting together an offer the network hopes will suffice those who are making the decisions on whether or not to expand the playoff. On the other hand, networks and streaming platforms outside Bristol are banking on conferences like the SEC and Big Ten not taking ESPN up on their offer, which would then take the CFP expansion to the open market. And yes, networks like FOX are hoping their contract with the Big Ten pays off by having these negotiations extend past October 9th, which would allow them to get in on the bidding. GREG SANKEY MAKES IT CLEAR THAT SEC DIDN’T START THE 16-TEAM CFP FORMAT DISCUSSION, THAT'S ON THE BIG TEN Now, I'm not implying that them, or streaming platforms, would come to the table with a sizable offer that would force CFP leaders to think twice about accepting ESPN's deal. These conferences are smart enough to already know what each network is willing to offer. Remember, SEC television rights are owned by the four-letter network, while the Big Ten is under contract with FOX. INSIDE THE SEC’S HIGH-STAKES DESTIN SHOWDOWN OVER CFP EXPANSION, NIL AND A POSSIBLE NCAA BREAKAWAY It just so happens that the two conferences who will end up making the final decision, thanks to the power bestowed upon them last year in an agreement with the Big 12, ACC, Notre Dame and G-6, are sitting on the opposite sides of what their television partners would be presenting. Remember, this is for the good of college football.... I would hope by now that fans of this cherished sport would see right through the nonsense that is being spewed through either backchannel communications or the interviews given over the course of the past year. This talk of expansion, which is more than just chatter at this point, essentially flipped within a three-month stretch dating back to CFP meetings around the national championship game last year in Miami. One minute, most are in agreement that a sixteen-team model would be the wise move. Then, after realizing how cash-strapped a large chunk of these schools were, the conversation shifted towards the Big Ten's idea of 24-teams. GREG SANKEY INSISTS SEC IS 'STRONGEST LEAGUE' DESPITE BIG TEN WINNING THREE STRAIGHT NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS The twelve-team format didn’t have a chance to be enjoyed before we were already discussing expansion, as if college football needs to resemble March Madness. "I was in the group that took it from four to 12 teams—and that was monumental," SEC commissioner Greg Sankey told John Ourand. "And it’s worked really well. I think the timing of that implementation was, if not perfect, as close to perfect as you’ll get. So we’re two years through the 12-team playoff. We put games on campus in the postseason for the first time at the FBS level. We haven’t been successful in the final game, but we’ve been better represented than any other conference. There are a lot of ideas, and our concerns relate to how you manage the economics. Is there value in 24 or not? "I don’t think people understand the difficulty of going week to week to week to week in December. … We’ve looked at it and said CFP selection decisions are negatively impacting regular-season scheduling, particularly big non-conference games. That needs to be addressed first, and also the economics, what we do with conference championship games, where the games fit, and understanding the impact." It's not just as simple as accepting a deal from a television network But, there are plenty of people who want to make you think that more teams will create stronger parity in the sport, which will then force teams to increase their budgets to compete on a yearly basis. For this to happen, expanding the CFP, conferences will have to get rid of championship weekend. This means, the SEC would have to buy its way out of contracts with companies like Regions, Dr. Pepper, Allstate, Bush's Beans, Johnsonville, Mercedes-Benz Stadium and a plethora of others who signed deals to sponsor the event. EXCLUSIVE: CLARK LEA SAYS COLLEGE FOOTBALL WILL HAVE TO SACRIFICE TRADITION IN EXCHANGE FOR CFP EXPANSION And, don't forget about the money made from the game itself, which grosses around $100 million for the conference, with a television deal with ESPN included. The same can be said for the Big Ten, who plays their title game inside Lucas Oil Stadium every year, and provides a major economic impact for the city of Indianapolis. When the 'Protect College Sports Act' inserted a new amendment that would essentially double the amount of money each school was allowed to spend, from around $22 million to upwards of $45 million, the writing was on the wall. And please, save us with the talk of how this is only going to strengthen the sport of college football. There aren’t 24-teams worthy of vying for a national championship. Heck, there aren’t 16 teams who are truly capable of hoisting a CFP trophy at seasons end. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP And where exactly are they going to get this money? Are they striking oil in Kentucky or Iowa? Did Walmart all the sudden start funding the Arkansas football roster without us paying attention? Is Texas Tech booster Cody Campbell going to start helping out other schools in the state so they can compete on a yearly basis? No. This feels more like the 2008 financial crisis where the government decided a cash-infusion could help stabilize the market, this time in the form of a television agreement that leads to more teams making the postseason. Just because you slap a CFP logo on a first round game that pits James Madison against Virginia Tech doesn’t mean it will equal ratings. We'll see what transpires over the next two months, as the December 1st deadline looms for a decision on expansion. I look forward to those teams who are eliminated in the first round of a 24-team playoff with an 8-5 record hanging a CFP banner in the practice facility.
news.summary: The College Football Playoff committee awaits ESPN's formal offer on expansion to 24 teams, but conference championship contracts complicate the deal.
